items.stem: Which arrangement in the Brexit withdrawal deal avoided a hard border on the island of Ireland?
items.answer: The Northern Ireland Protocol (later amended by the Windsor Framework)
items.markingKey: The Northern Ireland Protocol (later amended by the Windsor Framework). The Protocol kept Northern Ireland aligned with EU goods rules, creating checks in the Irish Sea.

items.stem: Distinguish between a virtual border and a physical border.
items.answer: A physical border is a territorial line, often marked by fences, posts or checkpoints; a virtual border operates through digital data and remote checks, which may take place far from the frontier.
items.markingKey: A physical border is a territorial line, often marked by fences, posts or checkpoints; a virtual border operates through digital data and remote checks, which may take place far from the frontier. items.stem: Zara writes: "Globalisation has made borders irrelevant." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Goods, capital and data cross borders more easily, but states have built more walls and fences since 2000 and border controls tightened sharply during COVID-19.
items.markingKey: Goods, capital and data cross borders more easily, but states have built more walls and fences since 2000 and border controls tightened sharply during COVID-19. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source A
When the Berlin Wall fell in 1989, many expected walls between states to disappear in a globalising world. Instead, the number of border walls and fences around the world has grown from about 15 at that time to more than 70.
— Élisabeth Vallet, ed., Borders, Fences and Walls: State of Insecurity? (2014; updated figures 2022) (paraphrased)

With reference to Source A, explain why the trend in the source might be described as a paradox of globalisation. [3]
items.answer: Globalisation was expected to open borders, yet states have built more physical barriers in response to migration, terrorism and insecurity, showing that interdependence has been accompanied by a reassertion of territorial control.
items.markingKey: Globalisation was expected to open borders, yet states have built more physical barriers in response to migration, terrorism and insecurity, showing that interdependence has been accompanied by a reassertion of territorial control. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: "Physical border barriers are an effective response to irregular migration." With reference to specific examples, discuss this statement. [15]
items.answer: Barriers can reduce crossings locally but tend to displace rather than stop migration, at high human cost.

items.stem: Using Russia’s annexation of Crimea (2014) as an example, explain the challenge of border changes by force to international order.

The annexation violated the norm against acquiring territory by force and led to sanctions and the wider war of 2022.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "International law is ineffective in resolving border disputes."
items.answer: International law is effective where states consent, but weak against powerful states determined to change borders by force.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: China rejected the 2016 South China Sea ruling; Russia annexed Crimea despite UN resolutions; no enforcement mechanism. Arguments against: ICJ rulings settled disputes (e.g. Cameroon–Nigeria, Bakassi, 2002); UNCLOS provides a framework for maritime claims; legal rulings shape legitimacy and alliances. Supported judgement: International law is effective where states consent, but weak against powerful states determined to change borders by force.

items.stem: Using border closures during COVID-19 (2020) as an example, explain the resilience of state control over borders.
items.answer: Most states restricted entry; Australia and New Zealand largely closed their borders to non-citizens, and even Schengen states reimposed internal controls. The pandemic showed that, in a crisis, states reassert sovereign control over borders, even within integrated regions.
items.markingKey: Context (Most states restricted entry; Australia and New Zealand largely closed their borders to non-citizens, and even Schengen states reimposed internal controls.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The pandemic showed that, in a crisis, states reassert sovereign control over borders, even within integrated regions. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the resilience of state control over borders.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the UK–Rwanda asylum plan (2022–2024) shows the tension between border control and international refugee law.
items.answer: The UK planned to send asylum seekers to Rwanda; the UK Supreme Court ruled it unlawful in 2023 because of the risk of refoulement, and the new government cancelled it in 2024. The courts upheld non-refoulement against a policy designed to deter arrivals, showing legal limits on state sovereignty over borders.
items.markingKey: Context (The UK planned to send asylum seekers to Rwanda; the UK Supreme Court ruled it unlawful in 2023 because of the risk of refoulement, and the new government cancelled it in 2024.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Borders are becoming less significant in global politics."
items.answer: Borders are changing in form rather than declining; states have reasserted control in new ways.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Schengen and free movement; digital economy and capital flows; transnational challenges (climate, pandemics). Arguments against: walls and fences have multiplied since 1989; COVID-19 border closures; Brexit and migration politics show the salience of borders. Supported judgement: Borders are changing in form rather than declining; states have reasserted control in new ways.

items.stem: "States’ right to control their borders should take priority over the rights of migrants." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: States may regulate entry, but their right is limited by binding obligations to protect refugees and human rights.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: sovereignty and democratic consent; security and public order; welfare and labour market concerns. Arguments against: non-refoulement and human rights law; most migration benefits host economies; restrictive policies push migrants into dangerous routes. Supported judgement: States may regulate entry, but their right is limited by binding obligations to protect refugees and human rights. items.stem: Examine the view that international law is ineffective in resolving border disputes. Use relevant key concepts and named examples in your answer. [15]
items.answer: International law is effective where states consent, but weak against powerful states determined to change borders by force.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: China rejected the 2016 South China Sea ruling; Russia annexed Crimea despite UN resolutions; no enforcement mechanism. Arguments against: ICJ rulings settled disputes (e.g. Cameroon–Nigeria, Bakassi, 2002); UNCLOS provides a framework for maritime claims; legal rulings shape legitimacy and alliances. Possible judgement: International law is effective where states consent, but weak against powerful states determined to change borders by force. items.stem: In which valley did Indian and Chinese troops clash in June 2020, killing 20 Indian soldiers?
items.answer: The Galwan Valley
items.markingKey: B. It was the first deadly clash on the LAC since 1975; China acknowledged four deaths.

items.stem: Define the term "virtual border".
items.answer: Border control carried out away from the physical frontier through digital systems such as visa databases, biometric checks and advance passenger information
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: border control carried out away from the physical frontier through digital systems such as visa databases, biometric checks and advance passenger information. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "internally displaced person (IDP)"?
options: The principle of international law that refugees must not be returned to a country where they face serious threats to their life or freedom
A person forced to flee their home who remains within their own country’s borders
The 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, which defines territorial seas (12 nautical miles) and exclusive economic zones (200 nautical miles)
A boundary created by customs, tariffs and regulations, such as the external tariff of the EU customs union
items.answer: A person forced to flee their home who remains within their own country’s borders
items.markingKey: B. "internally displaced person (IDP)" is a person forced to flee their home who remains within their own country’s borders.

items.stem: Distinguish between de facto borders and de jure borders.
items.answer: De jure borders are legally recognised, often by treaty; de facto borders reflect actual control on the ground, such as the LAC or lines of occupation.
items.markingKey: De jure borders are legally recognised, often by treaty; de facto borders reflect actual control on the ground, such as the LAC or lines of occupation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Globalisation has made borders irrelevant." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Goods, capital and data cross borders more easily, but states have built more walls and fences since 2000 and border controls tightened sharply during COVID-19.
items.markingKey: Goods, capital and data cross borders more easily, but states have built more walls and fences since 2000 and border controls tightened sharply during COVID-19. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why most refugees are hosted in neighbouring, low- and middle-income countries.
items.answer: Refugees flee to the nearest safe place and often lack means to travel further; rich states restrict access through visas and border controls, so countries such as Türkiye, Colombia, Uganda and Pakistan host large numbers.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Refugees flee to the nearest safe place and often lack means to travel further; rich states restrict access through visas and border controls, so countries such as Türkiye, Colombia, Uganda and Pakistan host large numbers. items.stem: Explain why borders matter to state sovereignty.
items.answer: Borders define the territory within which a state claims supreme authority; controlling who and what crosses them is a core expression of sovereignty, as the Brexit slogan “take back control” emphasised.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Borders define the territory within which a state claims supreme authority; controlling who and what crosses them is a core expression of sovereignty, as the Brexit slogan “take back control” emphasised. items.stem: A student claims: "States can return any asylum seeker to their country of origin." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Non-refoulement forbids returning refugees to places where they face persecution, torture or serious harm; it is considered part of customary international law.
items.markingKey: Non-refoulement forbids returning refugees to places where they face persecution, torture or serious harm; it is considered part of customary international law. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe Russia’s annexation of Crimea (2014) and explain what it reveals about the challenge of border changes by force to international order.
items.answer: After a disputed referendum held under Russian military presence, Russia annexed Crimea; the UN General Assembly (Resolution 68/262) affirmed Ukraine’s territorial integrity. The annexation violated the norm against acquiring territory by force and led to sanctions and the wider war of 2022.
items.markingKey: Context (After a disputed referendum held under Russian military presence, Russia annexed Crimea; the UN General Assembly (Resolution 68/262) affirmed Ukraine’s territorial integrity.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The annexation violated the norm against acquiring territory by force and led to sanctions and the wider war of 2022. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the challenge of border changes by force to international order.

items.stem: Using the Windsor Framework (2023) as an example, explain the political complexity of economic borders.
items.answer: The UK and EU agreed to reduce checks on goods moving from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, with “green” and “red” lanes. The case shows how economic borders interact with identity and peace processes, requiring creative compromises.

items.stem:
Source D
No Contracting State shall expel or return a refugee in any manner whatsoever to the frontiers of territories where his life or freedom would be threatened on account of his race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion.
— 1951 Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees, Article 33(1) (extract)

With reference to Source D, explain how the source limits state sovereignty over borders. [4]
items.answer: Non-refoulement obliges states not to return refugees to danger, so states cannot simply exclude or deport people at will; sovereignty over entry is constrained by a legal duty of protection.
items.markingKey: Non-refoulement obliges states not to return refugees to danger, so states cannot simply exclude or deport people at will; sovereignty over entry is constrained by a legal duty of protection. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: Using the Galwan Valley clash (June 2020) as an example, explain the political consequences of border disputes.
items.answer: Indian and Chinese troops fought with clubs and stones at high altitude; 20 Indian and at least four Chinese soldiers died; India banned Chinese apps including TikTok. The clash hardened Indian policy towards China, affecting trade, technology and India’s alignment with the Quad.

items.stem: Examine the view that climate change will make the 1951 Refugee Convention obsolete. Use relevant key concepts and named examples in your answer. [15]
items.answer: The Convention is not obsolete but needs complementary protection for climate-related displacement.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: climate displacement is not covered by the Convention; growing numbers displaced by disasters; Teitiota v New Zealand (2020) recognised future risk. Arguments against: most climate displacement is internal; the Convention can apply when climate interacts with persecution or conflict; regional instruments (Kampala Convention) fill gaps. Possible judgement: The Convention is not obsolete but needs complementary protection for climate-related displacement. items.stem: "Border disputes are the most significant threat to peace in Asia." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Border disputes are among the most dangerous threats because of great-power and nuclear dimensions, though internal conflicts cause more immediate harm.
